It includes an analysis of minimal risk and maximum acceptable indoor temperatures for various cities, based on evidence from multiple studies. For example: In Boston, the minimal risk indoor temperature is 21–22°C, and the maximum acceptable temperature is 25°C. Studies by Nguyen et al. (2013, 2016) highlight a stable indoor temperature year-round and a linear relationship between indoor and outdoor temperatures above 21°C. In New York, the minimal risk indoor temperature is 22–24°C, and the maximum acceptable temperature is 27–28°C. Research by Quinn et al. (2014) and Uejio et al. In London and Manchester, the minimal risk indoor temperature is 22–23°C, with a maximum acceptable temperature of approximately 25°C. Wright et al. (2005) studied dwelling temperatures during the 2003 heatwave. In Harbin, the minimal risk indoor temperature is around 24°C, and the maximum acceptable temperature is 26°C. Wang et al. (2010) analyzed thermal responses in naturally ventilated buildings, noting similar indoor and outdoor temperatures during summer. In South Korea, the minimal risk temperature is 25–26°C, and the maximum acceptable temperature is 29–30°C. Studies by Kim et al. (2012) and Moon et al. In Thailand, the minimal risk temperature is approximately 30°C, and the maximum acceptable temperature is 32°C. Research by Wong and Li (2007) and Nguyen and Dockery (2016) examined naturally ventilated buildings and indoor-outdoor temperature relationships. The publication also references numerous studies on indoor air quality, thermal comfort, and the effects of high indoor temperatures on health, particularly among vulnerable populations such as the elderly and low-income groups. These studies span diverse geographic regions, including Africa, Asia, Europe, and North America, and provide evidence for the development of WHO guidelines on housing and health.
